lines.text: What if every nitrogen molecule in the air was swapped for argon?
At first, nothing seems to happen. Both gases are invisible, and your lungs mostly ignore them.
But argon is heavier. The whole sky now weighs about a third more.
Air pressure jumps, and everyone's ears pop at once.
Argon is also more narcotic than nitrogen.
At this pressure, some people feel slightly tipsy, like scuba divers going deep.
Sound travels a little slower through the heavier air.
So voices and music sound a touch deeper.
Fires change too. Argon soaks up less heat than nitrogen, so flames burn hotter.
Stoves roar, and wildfires race up the hills.
Then the real problem. Every living thing needs nitrogen to build proteins and DNA.
Bacteria and lightning used to pull it from the air. Now there's nothing to pull.
Factories can't make fertilizer either, and fertilizer helps feed about half the world.
Year by year, the soil runs low, and harvests shrink.
Soil bacteria still breathe a little nitrogen back into the air, but it's a trickle against an ocean.
Would we survive on a planet with no nitrogen to spare?
